Hi! I'm Vansh - Erasmus Master's student, a background in Electrical Engineering and couple of  years of software engineering experience at Amazon and Nvidia. I have experience in Python, machine learning, time-series forecasting and backend development. 

I'm interested in using NASA satellite data and AI to help farmers adapt to climate change. Looking for teammates with skills in agriculture, GIS, geospatial data, satellite imagery and frontend development. Let's build something impactful!
summary:
FARMS is a free web app that helps farmers in Lusatia, eastern Germany, choose crop rotations that will still work as summers get hotter and drier. Hot days at our test fields have tripled since 1985, and the sandy soils hold very little water, so many farms are growing crops that no longer fit their field.

A farmer picks a field, taps what matters most (saving water, soil health, income or livestock) and gets three options: today’s rotation, an easy small step and a bigger shift. Each comes with a score, the reasons, the risks and what to check locally. The farmer can also test what happens if summers get drier or warmer.

Eight NASA datasets (SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GRACE-FO, GLDAS, POWER and SRTM) and ESA Sentinel-2 power the app, including a machine-learning model trained on more than 13,000 crop fields. FARMS tests about 2,000 rotations per field in the real weather of 2015 to 2025, and we checked the NASA weather data against a German Weather Service station. On a real maize field near Luckau, the score rises from 21 to 68. The method is not tied to Lusatia: one command adds any new field in Germany or nearby countries in about seven minutes.
details:
The problem
In Lusatia, eastern Germany, hot days have tripled since 1985, sandy soils hold as little as 46 mm of water for roots, and NASA’s GRACE satellites show the region’s water storage falling. Farmers plan rotations years ahead, so they need evidence for their own field. FARMS answers the Field Shift challenge with exactly that.

What it does
The farmer picks a field and taps what matters most: saving water, soil health, income or livestock. The current rotation is pre-filled from EU satellite crop maps, so no typing is needed. FARMS compares three options: the current rotation, an easy “small step” (at most two crops changed) and a “bigger shift”. Each gets a score from 0 to 100, a year-by-year plan with cover crops, and plain-language notes: why, benefits, risks, information gaps and what to check locally.

The app also shows traffic-light cards for the field’s main risks (late frost, heat, water gap, soil water store, bare soil, heavy rain), when current crops are most exposed, a stress map of 1,254 crop fields in 2018 and 2022, climate trends since 1981, and “what if” sliders for less rain and more heat.

How it works

  • Data: eight NASA datasets: SMAP (soil moisture), GPM IMERG (rain), MODIS (greenness, dry air), ECOSTRESS (plant water stress), GRACE-FO (groundwater), GLDAS (temperature), POWER (daily weather) and SRTM (land height). Plus ESA Sentinel-2 (bare soil, 10 m), EU crop-type maps and SoilGrids soil data. The model’s inputs share one 250 m grid.
  • Model: a LightGBM model trained on more than 13,000 crop fields in Germany and nearby countries learned how weather and soil affect crop health. It beat linear regression and a neural network. In tests on areas about 100 km away, NASA weather data made it about 2.5 times more accurate (R² 0.19 → 0.50). On unseen Lusatia fields, R² is 0.48. Its ranges cover 79% of real results, and SHAP shows which factors mattered.
  • Rotation engine: for each field, FARMS tests about 2,000 four-year plans in the real weather of 2015 to 2025 and scores seven goals (reliability, water, soil health, erosion, pest break, income, forage), weighted by the farmer’s priorities. Crop water needs follow the FAO-56 standard, and every plan follows real farming rules (for example, a legume at least every four years).
  • Checked on the ground: against the German Weather Service station in Cottbus (1991 to 2025), NASA temperature matches almost perfectly (r = 0.998) and rain matches well (r = 0.89). NASA data misses some heavy downpours, and the app says so.

Example
A maize-only field near Luckau scores 21. The small step keeps two years of maize, scores 57, needs about 100 mm less extra water a year and keeps the soil covered in winter. The bigger shift scores 68.

Impact
FARMS helps farmers and advisers (such as Brandenburg’s LELF) adapt to drought, protect sandy soils and lower risk in bad years. It is free, open source and needs no login. It scales easily: one command adds any field in Germany or nearby countries in about seven minutes, and since NASA data is global and the EU crop maps cover Europe, it can be retrained for any EU region. Next: 10 m zones inside fields, more years of crop data and testing with farmers.

What makes it creative
It turns satellite data into a decision, not just a map. The small step matches how farmers really change: gradually, keeping their machines and markets. It replays real past seasons instead of one forecast, and always shows how sure it is.

What we considered
Real farm limits (irrigation, livestock or biogas, machinery, markets, crops they can’t grow), honest uncertainty and trade-offs, warnings outside the training area, data limits (coarse GRACE and POWER, only two years of crop labels), and plain language. FARMS supports the farmer’s judgement; it never replaces it.

Tools
Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, LightGBM, scikit-learn, SHAP, Plotly, Folium; Google Earth Engine, the NASA AppEEARS and POWER APIs, German Weather Service open data; GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud. No hardware.
